articles.label: Government Spending
articles.headline: Escambia County's $4.2 million tourism contract renewed without competitive bid
articles.dek: The deal with a Tallahassee marketing firm has rolled over three times since 2019. Commissioners say they're satisfied with the results. Public records show no formal performance review.
brief: Escambia County Commission approved a $4.2 million annual contract with Sachs Media for tourism marketing without seeking competitive bids
The contract has been renewed three consecutive times since 2019, totaling more than $25 million in public spending
Public records requests revealed no formal performance metrics or third-party audits evaluating the firm's work
articles.body:
The vote took 47 seconds. No discussion. No questions from the dais. On May 15, the Escambia County Commission approved another year with Sachs Media, the Tallahassee firm that has managed the county's tourism marketing since 2019.

The contract is worth $4.2 million annually. It has now rolled over three times without the county soliciting competing proposals.

"We're happy with what they're doing," Commission Chairman Jeff Bergosh said after the meeting. "The beaches are full. The hotels are booked. I don't see a reason to fix what isn't broken."

But a review of public records obtained by The Flightline shows the county has never conducted a formal performance evaluation of the contract. There are no documented metrics tying Sachs Media's campaigns to measurable tourism outcomes. No third-party audit has assessed whether the $25.8 million spent since 2019 delivered value proportional to the investment.

How the contract works

Escambia County collects a 5% tourist development tax on short-term lodging. That money funds beach renourishment, sports tourism facilities, and destination marketing. The marketing portion flows to Sachs Media under an agreement first signed in September 2019.

The original contract included two one-year renewal options. The county exercised both. In 2022, commissioners approved a new three-year agreement with the same renewal structure. No competitive solicitation accompanied any of these decisions.

Florida law does not require counties to competitively bid professional services contracts. But the county's own procurement policy recommends competitive selection for agreements exceeding $1 million "when practicable."

Asked why the county did not seek competing proposals, Bergosh pointed to continuity.

"You don't want to start over with someone new who doesn't understand the market," he said. "Sachs knows Pensacola. They know our beaches. That institutional knowledge has value."

What the records show

The Flightline submitted public records requests to Escambia County in March seeking all documents related to Sachs Media's performance, including internal evaluations, reports to commissioners, and any third-party assessments.

The county produced 214 pages of records. They included invoices, campaign summaries prepared by Sachs Media, and media placement reports showing where ads ran. The materials contained reach and impression statistics—how many people theoretically saw the ads.

Missing from the records: any county-generated analysis of whether those impressions translated to visitors. No surveys. No economic impact studies. No comparison of Pensacola's tourism growth against peer markets or statewide trends.

Sachs Media's own reports to the county cite rising visitor numbers and hotel occupancy rates. But those figures come from Visit Pensacola, the county's tourism arm, which works directly with Sachs. The relationship creates a feedback loop where the contractor's performance is measured by data the contractor helps contextualize.

"That's not an independent evaluation," said Jordan Wilcox, a public administration professor at the University of West Florida. "Best practice would be bringing in someone outside the relationship to assess whether the spending achieved its goals."

The county's position

County Administrator Wes Moreno defended the arrangement in an emailed statement.

"Escambia County continuously monitors all vendor contracts to ensure deliverables are met," Moreno wrote. "Tourism marketing is particularly difficult to measure in isolation, as visitor decisions are influenced by many factors beyond any single campaign."

He noted that tourism tax collections have increased 34% since 2019, from $18.7 million to $25.1 million in fiscal year 2025.

But tourism tax revenue rose across Florida during that period. Statewide collections increased 41% between 2019 and 2024, according to the Florida Department of Revenue. Escambia County's growth trailed the state average.

Commissioner Lumon May, who voted to approve the renewal, said he trusted staff recommendations.

"I rely on our professionals to vet these things," May said. "If there was a problem, I'd expect them to flag it."

Commissioner Steven Barry did not respond to requests for comment. Commissioners Mike Kohler and Robert Bender declined to discuss the contract beyond confirming their votes.

Industry comparisons

Other Florida counties handle tourism marketing differently. Bay County, home to Panama City Beach, uses a competitive RFP process every five years for its destination marketing contract. Okaloosa County conducts annual performance reviews with specific benchmarks tied to website traffic, booking conversions, and visitor surveys.

"You need accountability mechanisms built into any contract this size," said Rachel Donovan, executive director of the Florida Association of Counties' tourism council. "It protects the public investment. It also protects the vendor—gives them clear targets to hit."

Sachs Media did not respond to multiple requests for comment submitted by phone and email over two weeks.

What happens next

The current contract runs through September 2027 with two additional renewal options. If exercised, Sachs Media could continue managing Escambia County's tourism marketing through 2029 without a competitive process—a full decade under the same arrangement.

No commissioner has publicly called for a performance audit or competitive solicitation. The Tourist Development Council, an advisory board that recommends how tourism taxes are spent, has not placed the contract on its agenda for review.

The county's annual budget hearing begins in July. Tourism marketing spending will be included in the proposed budget, but individual contracts are not typically debated line by line during those sessions.

Bergosh said he would consider a formal review "if someone brought forward a specific concern."

"But right now," he said, "I'm looking at full hotels and crowded beaches. Hard to argue with that."

articles.label: Investigation
articles.headline: Who owns the last mile of Perdido Key?
articles.dek: As Alabama developers eye the state line, a patchwork of LLCs, family trusts and out-of-state investors control the undeveloped parcels. A Flightline investigation maps the ownership and the stakes.
brief: Escambia County property records reveal 23 distinct entities control the 847 acres of undeveloped land between the state line and the Perdido Key State Park boundary
At least 14 of those entities trace to out-of-state addresses, with registered agents in Texas, Georgia and Tennessee
Three parcels totaling 112 acres changed hands in the past 18 months at prices averaging $2.1 million per acre—triple the 2021 rate
articles.body:
The sand at the end of Perdido Key Drive is the same white powder that sells for $800 a night a half-mile east. But here, where Florida ends and Alabama begins, the dunes sit empty. No towers. No tiki bars. Just sea oats bending in the wind and a chain-link fence marking private property.

That fence belongs to Coastal Holdings Gulf LLC, a Delaware-registered entity with a mailing address in Houston. The company paid $4.2 million for its 31-acre parcel in March 2025. Before that, the land belonged to a Pensacola family trust that had held it since 1986.

Coastal Holdings Gulf is one of 23 entities that control what remains of undeveloped Perdido Key—847 acres stretching from the state line to the western boundary of Perdido Key State Park. The Flightline spent three months tracing deed records, corporate filings and tax rolls to identify who owns this land and where they're based.

What emerged is a portrait of a coastline in transition. Local families who bought cheap decades ago are cashing out. Private equity and regional developers are buying in. And the question of what gets built on Florida's last undeveloped barrier island shore is being decided in boardrooms far from Escambia County.

The ownership map

Escambia County property records identify 31 parcels of undeveloped or minimally developed land in the study area. The Flightline consolidated parcels with common ownership, revealing 23 distinct controlling entities.

Fourteen trace to out-of-state addresses. Texas leads with five entities, followed by Georgia with four. Tennessee, North Carolina and Delaware account for the rest. The Delaware registrations—Coastal Holdings Gulf among them—are particularly opaque. Delaware corporate law allows companies to shield beneficial ownership from public filings.

Nine entities list Florida addresses. Three are family trusts with Pensacola connections. Four are LLCs registered to addresses in Jacksonville, Tampa and Miami. Two list local registered agents but provided no other identifying information in their annual reports.

The largest single landowner is Old River Properties LP, a limited partnership registered in Atlanta. Old River controls 187 acres across four parcels, including the highest-elevation land on the key—a ridge that tops out at 23 feet above sea level. The company acquired its holdings between 2018 and 2022 at a combined cost of $28.6 million, according to deed stamps.

Old River's general partner is listed as Southeastern Coastal Ventures LLC. Georgia corporate records show that company is managed by Trent Holcomb, a real estate attorney in Alpharetta. Holcomb did not respond to three phone messages and an email seeking comment.

The price escalation

Land on Perdido Key has always been expensive. It's now approaching stratospheric.

Three parcels totaling 112 acres sold between January 2025 and this month. The Flightline calculated per-acre prices from deed stamps recorded with the Escambia County Clerk.

The Coastal Holdings Gulf parcel sold for $2.07 million per acre. A 54-acre tract that sold to Emerald Coast Land Partners LLC in October 2025 went for $2.3 million per acre. A smaller 27-acre parcel near the Oyster Bar Marina sold this month for $1.89 million per acre.

For comparison: in 2021, undeveloped Perdido Key land averaged $680,000 per acre, according to a market analysis prepared for Escambia County's land-use planning department. The analysis, obtained through a public records request, noted that prices had been "relatively stable" since 2017.

They are no longer stable.

"What you're seeing is scarcity pricing," said Marcus Webb, a commercial real estate broker with NAI Pensacola who has handled barrier island transactions. "There's no more Perdido Key being made. The state park isn't selling. And Alabama is about to put 2,000 condo units a mile west of the state line."

Webb was referring to Perdido Pass Resort, a $1.2 billion mixed-use development approved by Orange Beach in 2024. The project will add hotel rooms, condominiums and commercial space to the Alabama coastline immediately adjacent to Florida.

"That development changes the math for every parcel on the Florida side," Webb said. "You're not buying empty beach anymore. You're buying beach next to a destination."

The family trusts

Not everyone is selling.

The Mackey Family Trust controls 73 acres near the intersection of Perdido Key Drive and River Road. The land has been in the family since 1958, when Harold Mackey Sr. bought it for $12,000—about $130,000 in today's dollars.

Harold Mackey Jr., 71, serves as trustee. He lives in a single-story house on a two-acre slice of the property. The rest sits undeveloped, covered in slash pines and saw palmetto.

"I get calls every month," Mackey said. "Letters too. Some of them from people I've never heard of, some from companies that don't seem to exist when you look them up."

He showed a stack of correspondence at his kitchen table. Handwritten letters. Typed offers on law firm letterhead. A postcard from a "motivated buyer" with a Phoenix area code.

"My daddy told me this land would be worth something someday," Mackey said. "I think he was right. But worth something and worth selling are two different things."

Mackey said he has no plans to develop the property or sell it. The trust documents, he said, require unanimous consent from his three children before any sale. His oldest daughter lives in Seattle. She's never seen the land.

"She doesn't understand what it is," Mackey said. "She sees numbers. I see where my brother and I used to fish."

Two other family trusts—the Sandifer Trust and the Beachview Family Partnership—control a combined 91 acres. Neither trustee responded to interview requests.

The development pressure

Escambia County's comprehensive plan designates most of undeveloped Perdido Key as "coastal high hazard area." Development is permitted but subject to density limits, setback requirements and stormwater restrictions.

In practice, that means any large-scale project requires variances, plan amendments or both.

County records show three pre-application meetings for Perdido Key projects since January 2025. The meetings are confidential under Florida law, but county staff confirmed they occurred. Development Services Director Patricia Holman declined to identify the applicants or the parcels involved.

"I can tell you we're seeing more interest in that area than we've seen in years," Holman said. "Whether that turns into actual applications, I can't say."

Commissioner Jeff Bergosh, whose district includes Perdido Key, has been vocal about the need to preserve the area's character. At a February commission meeting, he proposed a moratorium on high-density development west of the state park.

"We're one of the last places on the Gulf Coast that isn't wall-to-wall condos," Bergosh said at the meeting. "That's worth protecting."

The moratorium proposal died for lack of a second. Commissioners Doug Underhill and Lumon May expressed concern about property rights implications. Commissioner May noted that restricting development could expose the county to takings claims.

"We can't tell people they can't use their land," May said. "That's not how this works."

The Alabama factor

The Perdido Pass Resort broke ground in Orange Beach three weeks ago.

The project sits on 340 acres at the western tip of Alabama's Gulf coast, less than a mile from the Florida state line. Plans call for 1,800 condominium units, a 300-room hotel, 85,000 square feet of retail and restaurant space, and a marina with 200 slips.

First units are projected to open in late 2028. Full buildout is scheduled for 2033.

"This is transformational for the region," said Brett McCaleb, CEO of Horizon Gulf Development, the project's lead developer. McCaleb spoke to The Flightline by phone from his office in Birmingham.

Asked whether Horizon has any interest in Florida parcels, McCaleb paused.

"We're focused on our current project," he said. "But we're always evaluating opportunities."

Corporate records show Horizon Gulf Development shares a registered agent with Emerald Coast Land Partners LLC—the company that paid $124 million for 54 acres on Perdido Key last October. The registered agent, a corporate services firm in Tallahassee, declined to confirm or deny any relationship between the entities.

What comes next

The 847 acres sit and wait.

Morning joggers pass the chain-link fences. Fishermen cast from the public beach access points between the private parcels. Real estate agents drive clients down Perdido Key Drive and point at the empty dunes, describing what could be.

At the Mackey property, Harold Mackey Jr. walks his land most evenings. He checks the fences. He watches for trespassers. He looks at the Gulf.

"They can buy the land next to me," he said. "They can build whatever they want. But this piece stays in the family."

He paused.

"At least while I'm still here."

The Flightline will continue tracking ownership changes and development applications on Perdido Key. Documents referenced in this investigation are available through the Escambia County Property Appraiser and Clerk of Court public records portals.

articles.label: Military
articles.headline: NAS Pensacola's summer flight schedule means more noise complaints—and a familiar standoff
articles.dek: Training operations peak in June. Residents near the base say the Navy's noise hotline goes nowhere. The Navy says it's doing what it can. The disconnect is decades old.
brief: NAS Pensacola flight operations typically increase 30-40% during summer training cycles, with June historically the busiest month
The base's noise complaint hotline logged over 2,400 calls in summer 2025, but residents say responses are generic and nothing changes
Navy officials point to flight path restrictions already in place and say the mission requirements leave little room for further accommodation
articles.body:
The T-6B Texan II banks hard over Perdido Bay at 7:14 on a Tuesday morning, engine whining at a pitch that cuts through double-pane windows and closed doors. In the Innerarity Point subdivision below, Karen Mulholland is already on her third cup of coffee. She stopped calling the Navy's noise hotline two years ago.

"They send you a form letter," Mulholland said. "Thank you for your concern. Training is essential. That's it. Every time."

Summer is coming to NAS Pensacola, and with it the annual surge in flight training that makes the base one of the busiest naval air stations in the country. Student pilots cycle through primary and intermediate training in waves, and June marks the peak. For the neighborhoods that ring the base—Warrington, Innerarity Point, parts of Perdido Key—the next three months will be the loudest of the year.

The tension between military mission and residential quality of life is older than most of the houses in those neighborhoods. It has never been resolved. There's no evidence it ever will be.

The numbers

NAS Pensacola conducts an average of 340,000 flight operations annually, according to the most recent data provided by base public affairs. That figure includes touch-and-go landings, which count as two operations each. Summer months typically see a 30-40% increase over the winter baseline, with June historically logging the highest totals.

The base's community relations office operates a noise complaint hotline that logged 2,417 calls between June 1 and August 31, 2025. That number was up from 2,089 the previous summer. The office did not provide data on how many individual callers those totals represent or what specific responses were issued.

Lt. Commander Jessica Ramirez, a public affairs officer at NAS Pensacola, said the base takes every complaint seriously.

"Each call is logged and reviewed," Ramirez said in an email response to questions. "When patterns emerge, we coordinate with training squadrons to evaluate whether adjustments are feasible within mission requirements."

Asked how many complaints had resulted in operational changes over the past five years, Ramirez said that information was not tracked in a way that could be easily reported.

What residents hear

Tom Brennan bought his house on Innerarity Point in 2019. He knew the base was there. He says he didn't understand what that would mean.

"The realtor said something about occasional training flights," Brennan said. "Occasional. That's the word she used."

On a recent weekday, Brennan counted 47 overflights between 7 a.m. and noon. He keeps a log now, has for two years. He brought a printout to a town hall meeting in Perdido Key last fall. He said a Navy representative nodded politely and thanked him for his engagement.

"Nothing changed," Brennan said. "Not one thing."

Residents in the affected areas describe a consistent pattern: calls to the hotline are answered, complaints are acknowledged, form letters arrive. The flights continue.

The Navy's position is that flight paths and training schedules are already constrained by safety requirements, airspace limitations and coordination with Pensacola International Airport. The T-6B training pattern, which takes student pilots over the bay and barrier islands, exists because other options would create conflicts with commercial traffic or require overflying more densely populated areas.

"We're not flying these routes arbitrarily," Ramirez said. "Every pattern is designed to minimize community impact while meeting training requirements that are not discretionary."

The legal landscape

Residents seeking relief through official channels face limited options. Military installations are exempt from local noise ordinances. The Federal Aviation Administration regulates airspace but does not set noise limits for military training operations. Florida state law provides no additional recourse.

A 1988 Supreme Court decision, United States v. Causby, established that persistent low-altitude military overflights can constitute a "taking" under the Fifth Amendment, potentially entitling property owners to compensation. But successful claims require proving that flights are so frequent and low as to render the property unusable—a high bar that most residential complaints don't meet.

Class action lawsuits against military bases have been attempted in other states with mixed results. No such action is currently pending against NAS Pensacola.

Escambia County Commissioner Jeff Bergosh, whose district includes some affected areas, said he regularly hears from constituents about noise but has limited ability to intervene.

"The base was here before most of these neighborhoods," Bergosh said. "That's the reality. People need to understand what they're buying into."

He added that the base's economic impact—an estimated $7.8 billion annually in the regional economy—means local officials are unlikely to push too hard.

"We're a Navy town," Bergosh said. "That comes with trade-offs."

No resolution in sight

The Navy has made some accommodations over the years. Training flights are prohibited between 10:30 p.m. and 6:30 a.m. except in emergencies. Certain residential areas are designated as "noise-sensitive" and pilots are instructed to avoid them when possible. The Blue Angels, based at NAS Pensacola, practice over the water rather than over populated areas.

But the fundamental conflict—a major training base surrounded by growing residential development—has no obvious solution. The base cannot relocate. The training cannot stop. The houses are already built.

Mulholland, the Innerarity Point resident, said she's made peace with it in her own way.

"I stopped fighting," she said. "I just wear earplugs in the morning now. It's easier than being angry all the time."

The noise hotline number is (850) 452-2345. The base asks callers to note the date, time and location of the disturbance. Responses typically arrive within two weeks.

Summer training operations at NAS Pensacola are scheduled to increase beginning June 2.
